question: The new import duties on Russian linseed are having a major impact on Belgian linseed processors. The Belgian processing sector accounts for almost half of the 700 000 tonnes of linseed processed each year in Europe. The bulk of it comes from Russia. 1.
What flanking measures does the Commission intend to take to minimise the impact on European linseed processors?
Is the Commission considering phasing in import duties so as to give the processing sector time to adapt its supply chain to this new situation?
answer: The measure proposed by the Commission to increase the tariffs on imports into the EU of grain products from Russia (1) has been put forward to prevent the destabilisation of the EU market caused by a potential redirection of Russian products onto the EU.
The measure covers linseed products as this is a grain product and, importantly, one of the top three where the most significant importation from Russia takes place at present.

The Commission notes that Belgium is the primary EU importer of these products as well as of increasing EU imports from Russia — up to 400 000 tonnes in 2023 — from much lower historic levels of about 230 000 tonnes during the 2020-2022 period. The recent growth in import from Russia has crowded out traditional world suppliers such as Kazakhstan and Canada.

However, despite the strong position established by Russia, the EU importers would be encouraged to turn to sourcing linseeds from these traditional suppliers or from the EU, thus reducing the EU dependency on Russia.

Given this increasing role of Russian linseed in EU grain markets and its ability to replace other oilseeds, the Commission believes that the non-inclusion of linseed would put the stability of EU markets at risk and, in addition, would create a significant loophole detrimental to the effectiveness of the proposed measure.

At the same time, the Commission actively supported the discussions in the Council and, as a result, the regulation (2) adopted by the Council of the European Union includes a solution that incentivises the establishment of alternative sourcing at competitive prices, while phasing in import duties on the products concerned gradually, until 31 December 2025, thus giving the processing sector the necessary time to adapt its supply chains.
